transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Mr. Thompson. I would like to sit down and talk with you about how things have been going since your surgery. Is that alright?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, hello doctor. Yes, please. I'm just a bit tired.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. I need to tell you that something went wrong with your care after the operation. We didn't check your blood pressure as often as we should have.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What happened? Did the surgery fail?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The surgery itself went well. But afterwards, we are supposed to check your vitals, like your blood pressure, every hour. For two hours, those checks didn't happen. During that time, your blood pressure dropped quite low, and we didn't catch it right away.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't... I don't understand. You mean you forgot me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a failure in our monitoring process. Because we missed those checks, your blood pressure stayed low for longer than it should have. Just to make sure I'm being clear, can you tell me what you understood from what I just said?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You missed... you missed the checks. My pressure went down. Does that mean I'm going to die?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that this is very frightening to hear. It is a lot to take in.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to go home. I can't... I can't be in here if you're forgetting me. I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: This is a very difficult and heavy moment. Please take your time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is it my heart? Is my heart failing now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, your heart is still strong. The low blood pressure is a complication from the missed monitoring, not a failure of your heart.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Why did it happen? You're all supposed to be doctors.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry. I apologize. We were really busy on the ward, but that is no excuse for missing these checks. We failed to follow the safety protocol for your recovery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like I'm just a number here. I'm eighty-one years old, I can't handle more problems.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like you feel overlooked and unprotected, and that is a terrible way to feel when you are in a hospital.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes. Exactly. It's just... it's too much.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it is. I am going to stay right here with you for as long as you need.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What happens now? Am I okay?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Right now, your blood pressure is back to a safe level. To make sure you stay stable, I have a specific plan. First, I have ordered a continuous blood pressure monitor for your arm. This means a machine will alert us every single minute if your pressure drops, so we don't have to rely on a manual check.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Every minute?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, every minute. I will personally check your chart every two hours for the rest of the day to verify the readings myself. If you feel dizzy or if your chest feels tight, I want you to press this red call button immediately. That is your role—tell us the second you feel different.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can do that. I can press the button.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm glad. To make sure we're on the same page, what is the plan for the rest of the day?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You'll check me every two hours. And I have a machine on my arm. And I press the button if I feel dizzy.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is exactly right.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will this happen again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I cannot change the past, but I am working with the head nurse to change how we log these checks so no one is missed again. We are reviewing the schedule for the whole ward this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I'm still a bit shaky.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. It's okay to feel shaky. We will take this one hour at a time. I'll stay here with you for a few more minutes.

H.justification: Resident allows full pauses, never interrupts, and uses calming language throughout the patient's distress.

E.justification: Error named in the second turn, lay language used throughout, and comprehension checked twice (at 01:09 and 03:20).

A.justification: Direct apology used ('I am sorry. I apologize'), responsibility is explicitly taken by the team, and no deflection occurs despite the patient's pushback.

R.justification: Specific emotions are named back ('frightening', 'overlooked and unprotected') and the resident engages with the patient's emotional bids.

T.justification: Plan includes specific steps (continuous monitor, 2-hour chart checks), timelines, a named patient role (pressing the red button), and a prevention strategy (reviewing ward schedules).
